projects.title: Local AI
projects.meta: Xeon E5-2680 v4 · 2× Tesla V100 32 GB
projects.desc_html: Fully local LLM inference stack — open-source models served on a pair of Tesla V100 32 GB cards by llama.cpp and the Strata engine, wrapped in a Hermes agent layer with a custom Discord frontend. Every measured run, table and write-up is published in the repo: github.com/EamonMcKiernan05/Local-LLM-Testing.

sections.label: Stack
items: 2× Tesla V100 32 GB linked at PCIe 3.0 ×16 — driver 580 pinned as the last Volta driver branch, CUDA 12.9, and llama.cpp rebuilt sm_70-only (144 embedded sm_70 cubins); the Strata engine built for sm_70 serves a 128K-context Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with MTP speculative decoding

Extended the box to NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B the day after upstream support merged: rebuilt llama.cpp from master to build 11700 (CUDA 12.9, sm_70 cubins) and served the 74B MoE at 262,144 ctx across both V100s with NVIDIA's separate 1.1B LiLiCorr drafter on llama.cpp's dflash speculative path — 128 of 490 draft tokens accepted and 53 tok/s decode on a prose prompt, against 139 tok/s on a counting test where drafting hits its ceiling

A third engine, Project Maya — GLM-5.3-Flash, a ~320B Mixture-of-Experts (~18B active) layer-split across both cards. The newest quant is a 313B-parameter, hand-mixed 87 GB IQ2_XXS whose publisher prunes the MTP block, so it benches with speculative drafting off: at the full 262,144-token window it holds 22.5–24.9 tok/s decode and 714 tok/s prefill at 20K rising to 870 at 200K (851 at 250K), every figure the mean of three fresh-load runs per depth, and engine v1.1.13 → v1.1.15 lifted prefill 7.6–10.3% at every depth while decode stayed inside its run-to-run spread. That window fits because the cache is streamed: a 32,768-position slice of each attention layer stays in VRAM (0.37 GB across both cards) while the other 88% of the 262K positions sit in 2.95 GB of pinned, device-mapped host RAM, and 93–99% of block reads still hit VRAM. Halving the window to 131K changes nothing measurable (+0.3% prefill / +2.6% decode at the shared depths) — long context is essentially free on this box. The Maya-S 321B quant, MTP drafting on, reads 20.4–22.6 tok/s decode and 595–646 tok/s prefill. Moving the model set off a DRAM-less boot SSD onto a dedicated NVMe was worth +23.9% decode / +46.0% prefill mean on a same-day, three-runs-per-side controlled pair.

Measured speculative decoding on that quant instead of assuming it pays: the GLM-5.3-Flash DFlash2 drafter (Q4_K_M, 697 MB, five layers) accepted 63% of its drafts and still ran 27–31% slower than the same engine without it — 15.9–18.0 tok/s decode against 22.5–24.9 — so drafting stays off for this model
Two-card tensor split with MTP; the full 262,144-token window runs end to end — a 250,632-token prompt prefilled at 1,495 tok/s, then 6,000 tokens generated at 48.8 tok/s

Cooling rebuilt around a single 7k-rpm PWM fan driven by a systemd hwmon fan curve — a ten-minute soak of six back-to-back 100k-token prefills held dead-flat at 61–62 °C (1,078 tok/s, 0.7 tok/s spread). Redesigned the 80 mm ducting into a mirrored one-fan-per-card pair — each fan 30 mm outboard of the stack, the cards’ original one-slot (40 mm) mouth spacing kept, and both meshes closed and single-body on export

sections.label: Current Numbers (October 2026)
items: Engine v0.1.32 → v0.1.39, same model and config byte-for-byte: decode +22–31% at every depth (20k: 56.6 → 73.9 tok/s; 250k: 50.3 → 65.0) and prefill +23–26% from 60k up (peak 1,973 tok/s at 100k)
126-run MTP sweep against the live server across all six depths: gate 0.50 confirmed fastest and the stock configuration measured fastest overall, with 250k-prompt prefill flat at 1,494–1,498 tok/s

model-bench harness for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint — browser UI + CLI, auto-detects llama.cpp or Strata, writes per-run JSONL/CSV/markdown; published at github.com/EamonMcKiernan05/Local-AI-Speed-Test-Harness
Enabled vision on the base model — the image encoder built locally for sm_70, verified with a real image read in 4.0 s at 93 tok/s decode
One-shot demo bench — single-prompt browser demos written by the local model: run them all in the demo gallery

projects.title: Media Server
projects.desc_html: Self-hosted media stack with a fully automated download pipeline, GPU transcoding on a GTX 1650 mapped into the app containers, and ZFS-backed redundant storage.

sections.label: Details
items: Sonarr, Radarr, and Prowlarr for automated media acquisition

Jellyfin on TrueNAS with the GTX 1650 passed into the app container — the card, its device nodes and NVIDIA's userspace libraries are all visible from inside it, and its bundled ffmpeg offers h264, hevc and av1 NVENC encoders plus CUDA decode
TrueNAS with ZFS for redundant storage and data integrity
TrueNAS replication for off-site backup of the media library
The same box also runs Nextcloud 35 as a self-hosted private cloud — PostgreSQL database and file data on separate host paths under the existing snapshot and replication coverage
Reverse proxied via Nginx Proxy Manager with HTTPS

sections.label: GPU Transcoding
items: Found Jellyfin's hardware acceleration switched off in its own settings — the config read HardwareAccelerationType: none while every read-only check said the GPU was available, so every stream had been transcoding on the CPU; enabled NVENC and re-read the config to confirm it took

Proved a catalog HandBrake app could never use that GPU, whatever its settings: the image is Alpine/musl and NVIDIA's encoder userspace is glibc-only, so ldd inside the container failed on a missing loader and the encoder library never opened — and the catalog template strips the device from both containers anyway, an upstream issue its own template flags

Stood up a glibc-based HandBrake image with an explicit GPU device reservation instead, and verified it inside the running container: nvidia-smi -L sees the GTX 1650 and HandBrakeCLI --help lists nvenc_h264 and nvenc_h265 with zero library-load errors

Diagnosed a crash-looping app install on the way: TrueNAS 25.04 creates app data folders root-owned while the containers run as uid 568, and its permissions helper now only checks rather than fixes — the container died on EACCES before it ever bound a port, while every app.start job still reported success

Worked out which encoder the card actually supports from NVIDIA's own matrix (TU117): H.264 4:2:0 and HEVC up to 10-bit encode, no H.264 10-bit encode or decode, no HEVC B-frames, no AV1 — so 10-bit sources go to HEVC and Hi10P falls back to the CPU

projects.title: Fantasy Football Isle of Man
projects.desc_html: FPL-style fantasy football game built for the Canada Life Premier League (Isle of Man). Full-stack application with FastAPI backend, web SPA, and a native iOS client integrating live match data from the FullTime API.

sections.label: Backend
items: FastAPI REST API with JWT authentication and bcrypt password hashing

Social sign-in (August 2026): Google and Apple OAuth consolidated onto a single shared Authlib layer — PKCE S256 with signed state cookies (no server session), JWKS-verified id_tokens (iss/aud/exp), Apple client_secret minted per exchange as an ES256 JWT, and user linking that keys on (provider, provider_id) before email to handle Apple's no-guaranteed-email and private-relay accounts; 31 new tests
SQLite + SQLAlchemy with Alembic migrations for schema management
FPL-style scoring engine with captain/vice-captain, transfers, and chips
APScheduler for automated gameweek scoring and data sync jobs
Position-based player scoring with performance-adjusted pricing

sections.label: Frontend & iOS App
items: Vanilla JS SPA with carousel-style page transitions, FPL-inspired design, and CSS custom property token system
Complete frontend redesign (2026): 14 dedicated page templates, modular JS architecture replacing monolithic app, matching official FPL site structure
Native iOS app built with SwiftUI (iOS 17+) – MVVM architecture with 18 views across 8 modules
Swift Concurrency (async/await) with URLSession actor and auto-refresh token rotation
Keychain Services for secure token persistence and session management
@Observable macro for reactive state management

sections.label: Security
items: Comprehensive security audit (July 2026): 18 files refactored, 22 vulnerabilities remediated and verified
Eliminated legacy auth bypass — all endpoints now enforce JWT-based authentication
Admin endpoints gated behind require_admin middleware with role-based access control
IDOR prevention: all state-mutating endpoints derive user identity from JWT, not client input
CORS restricted to APP_BASE_URL environment variable (was wildcard + credentials)
PKCE code_verifier stored in signed HttpOnly cookie instead of plain URL parameter
Rate limiting on login/register/refresh endpoints (5 req/min per IP)
Refresh tokens bound to user-agent string with HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict flags
Pydantic request schemas on all transfer endpoints preventing arbitrary key injection
Password policy enforcement: minimum 10 chars, uppercase + lowercase + digit required
Parameterized SQLite ATTACH DATABASE queries (prevented SQL injection via f-strings)
Database files removed from git history with *.db in .gitignore

sections.label: Data & DevOps
items: Live data pipeline syncing fixtures, results, and league tables from FullTime API
Separate database management service (FFIOM-DB) with automated data ingestion
GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline
Docker containerization: multi-container orchestration with separate API and database images, deployed to a dedicated Debian VM on Proxmox
Production deployment via Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared systemd service) with DNS routing to ffiom.com

Automated production updates: GitHub deploy key plus update script on the production VM pull the latest image from GitHub, take a pre-swap database backup, and health-verify the container swap (live-verified on ffiom.com)
Pytest test suite with production database isolation
App Store compliance: Info.plist hardening, ATS configuration, PrivacyInfo manifest, Keychain access groups

sections.label: FullTime Data Service
items: Self-hosted C# .NET 9 API on a dedicated Debian server, systemd-managed with Kestrel bound to the LAN — scrapes the Cloudflare-protected FullTime site with headless Chromium via Playwright, keeping the scraper warm with a persistent profile and a per-fetch cf_clearance cookie
Serves fixtures, results and league tables to the production app; maintained as a standalone service with reversible .bak backups of every changed file

sections.label: Quality Assurance
items: Full code review (August 2026): structured audit of the entire codebase — auth, scoring engine, scheduler, API routes, frontend, and deployment — run as parallel subagent reviews with a consolidated findings report

Remediated all 34 High/Medium/Low findings (10 High, 15 Medium, 9 Low): deterministic re-scoring, process locking on squad-mutation endpoints to prevent double-applied transfers, strict Content-Security-Policy on all 13 pages, and 14 new tests (138 → 152 passing)

Full production security audit (August 2026): tested all 106 live endpoints unauthenticated and as two fresh accounts, walked every UI page in a real browser, and inspected the production database directly — 0 critical, 6 high, 8 medium, 3 low findings, with all previously flagged criticals verified fixed in production

Remediated all 6 high + 8 medium audit findings (Aug 2026): access tokens moved to HttpOnly cookies so nothing token-related is JS-readable, full security-header set (CSP / HSTS / XFO / Referrer-Policy / Permissions-Policy), admin-gated a state-changing endpoint, disabled API docs in production, fixed corrupted gameweek state with a deadline guard, built the missing /account page, and closed user-enumeration — all verified end-to-end against copies of the live production database

projects.title: AI Trading Bot & Backtesting
projects.desc_html: AI-agent-driven trading system in two phases: a rigorous backtesting methodology (mechanical trend-following rules, realistic cost modelling, out-of-sample validation), then a production trading bot that ran the validated strategy live on Binance for 22 days — built to test whether disciplined rules beat buy-and-hold on real 2026 market data.

sections.label: Backtesting Engine
items: Python backtesting engine over real daily OHLC (Binance crypto, Yahoo stocks) with realistic costs: taker fees, funding-rate accrual, and overnight stock financing

Blind backtest: strategy rules committed to a written receipt before inspecting any price data — six sleeves (BTC/ETH/SOL 10x perp, NVDA/TSLA 5x long, COIN 5x short), daily hard stops, weekly trend filters, and earnings blackouts
Result: £100 → £135.85 (+35.9%) over ~8 months vs −14.5% for equal-weight buy-and-hold of the same six assets — the edge came from trend filters keeping capital out of three crashing crypto assets

sections.label: Validation
items: Top-50 crypto universe swept across 120 parameter combinations, then walk-forward validation: tuned on Jan–Apr, ran the single best config untouched on the unseen May–Aug window
Out-of-sample +16.5% vs +0.6% buy-and-hold — confirming the result was not a curve-fit artefact; all top-8 train configs clustered within £1.20 on the test window (robustness check)
Live paper trading: 10x BTC perpetual, +146.5% on £10 margin (take-profit exit), with full trade log and daily equity curve retained

sections.label: Live Trading Bot
items: Deployed the walk-forward-validated top-3 strategy (BTC/ETH/SOL, spot, long-only, no leverage) as a 24/7 production bot on a dedicated Debian LXC on the Proxmox cluster: SMA20 trend filter, 8% trailing stop, 3% fixed stop checked live on every 5-minute poll

Deterministic rules engine in pure Python (stdlib + requests only) — no improvisation: persistent state, unit tests, and a backtest-reproduction test asserting the validated engine’s exact £129.24 outcome (±0.5%)
Binance REST integration with a hard dry-run gate: real order code implemented but disabled until go-live; keys never committed (gitignored, chmod 600, wired only at go-live)
Single Docker image appliance: s6-overlay supervises the bot loop and a read-only web dashboard (GET-only, no exchange import), persistent data on a host bind mount, non-root

AI analysis bridge: trade events call a Hermes trading profile via API server; autonomous monitoring — a daily 06:00 agent-mode review pulls bot state and independently cross-checks live Binance prices (positions, armed stops, stop breaches, 7-day P&L vs buy-and-hold), plus a monthly review against the walk-forward baseline with an explicit strategy/investment verdict; documented go-live checklist

Went live with real funds (September 2026): first BTC order filled on Binance, then root-caused and fixed two live-only bugs — exchange info cached for the first symbol only (ETH/SOL rejected by LOT_SIZE) and MARKET fills recording a zero price — plus container-timezone and real-account-equity tracking fixes, all verified against the live API

Hardened the read-only dashboard after a live review of its charts: the klines endpoint was asking Binance for a single page (its 1,000-candle hard limit), so a 7-day per-minute view actually began just after midnight. The window is now walked backwards until it is covered or a 12,000-row cap is reached, and a granularity that cannot cover the chosen range says so in the hint line instead of quietly drawing less. Axis ticks moved onto natural steps (1/5/15/30 min through to 28 days) at round clock times, with the date added once a window crosses a day, and the page now fills the window rather than capping at 1200 px. Also fixed a destroyed-chart bug where one failed kline fetch left a dead reference that threw on the next resize and blanked the whole dashboard until a page reload — a transient exchange error could take monitoring down for the day; failures are now caught per section and self-heal on the next 60-second refresh

Ran live for 22 days on real funds (6–28 September 2026): funded $38.26, finished flat at $38.25 (−0.03%), then wound down deliberately — final real-account state snapshotted, the container stopped and verified unreachable, and auto-restart disabled so a reboot could not bring it back

sections.label: Decision-Model Evaluation (September 2026)
items: Screened a hosted decision model (TypeSafe’s Jev-1.13, a typed decision API rather than a chat model) as a candidate trading brain: a ten-cadence replay of the live bot’s own three-week window plus a three-month 5-minute replay — 113,000+ calls, 0.32–0.38s mean latency, ~$4.50 in total API spend. It underperformed buy-and-hold of the same three coins in both windows and acted on just 0.07–0.08% of the questions asked, so it stayed out of production.

Established the real break-even from Binance’s live order filters: at a $10 stake a BTC round trip needs a +8.65% move against a 0.25% mean hourly move (lot-step flooring and the $5 minNotional strand cash permanently), and lot-step dust alone stranded 13.2% of the sleeve across the three-month replay — at these stakes the binding cost is exchange mechanics, not the model.

Validated forward before trusting it: an 11-hour live paper run (1,993 calls, ten books at 1–10 minute cadences on real prices, $0.07 of spend) took one trade per book at near coin-flip confidence, and the negative result was written up with a corrections section, stated limits and a re-runnable harness rather than shelved — the live account kept its walk-forward-validated rules.

Extended the evaluation to its full window: a seven-month replay (Jan–Jul 2026, 61,056 five-minute ticks per book) at $60 and then $100 book sizes, the larger pass running four books side by side — control and rich state under the live mechanics and under a fee-aware buy guard — 243,797 Jev calls and $10.80 of spend, completed after a mid-run re-fill when the API provider's account-level budget cap cut the first pass short. It surfaced a genuine execution-mechanics defect: every sell floors to Binance's lot step, so a position bought with the last ~$5 of cash sits under the $5 minimum order once the fee is taken and can never be sold — the rich-state book under the live mechanics froze again, dead from May with three positions it could never sell (the same defect froze both $60 books), while the guarded book ended the window with zero trapped positions.

The verdict held at both book sizes and with the fix: in a window where the three coins fell 28–42%, no book beat buy-and-hold once unsellable lot-step dust was excluded — $12–35 of sellable value against $63.45 for simply holding, and the heaviest-churn book paid $12.72 in fees plus $70.82 stranded as unsellable dust across its 339 round trips.

Stress-tested whether a confidence gate could rescue it — offline, against the stored answers, so no new API calls: a gate sweep from 0.50 to 0.85, then a full buy×sell mixed grid. The higher gates "won" only by trading less (≥0.70 left 1 and 5 round trips across the seven months, mostly cash at $93.07 / $88.67), and the mixed grid showed no consistent sell-side effect — the flip-flopping signature of small-sample noise, not signal: 78% of the executed round trips came from 50–60% confidence buys at a 32% win rate, and only 16 buys in the entire window cleared P≥0.70. Read as what it is: the gate is an off-switch, not alpha.

Closed out the start-mode and rule-guard questions — a final pre-invested run plus offline sweeps against the stored answers: the pre-invested book ($33/coin bought at the 1 Jan close, managed from tick 0) finished at $66.25 of $99 against $63.79 for never trading, and a full cash-vs-invested gate grid confirmed every winning cell won by not participating. Hard rule overrides — take-profit, dip-exit with a re-entry lockout, and a trailing stop on each position's own peak with a rebound re-entry — all helped in the falling window (best settings: $66 → $96 against $63.79 for holding) and all lost in the rising one (the tightest guard turned the rise's $45 into $31, while doing nothing made $48): protection in a fall is the whipsaw tax in a rise.

sections.label: Further Strategy Studies (September 2026)
items: Tested the "hold while rising, cash while falling" filter family across five speeds (SMA20–SMA200 plus a 2% buffer band) as pre-committed rules on 2017→2026 daily closes: in the modern window it did not beat holding — pooled $300: best filter $1,724 vs $1,917 for buy-and-hold — while roughly halving drawdowns (BTC −53% → −32%, ETH −68% → −38%, SOL −76% → −58%) and dodging nearly the whole 2026 fall; the full-history version where the same rules win big ($5.6k–$29.4k vs $1.9k) is arithmetic from dodging 2018/2022, a structurally different era. Whipsaws were real — six switches in five weeks at BTC's late-2025 top — and a one-day execution lag moves finals 20–40%: recorded as crash insurance, not a wealth tool.

Encoded two "volume profile" setups from a trading thread — a value-area-low fakeout bounce and a thin-zone breakout — as pre-committed rules on cached 1-minute bars across matched falling and rising windows: 587 round trips with a weighted expectancy of −0.056% per trade before costs (a coin flip), the entire loss coming from fees ($95.86) and lot-size stranding ($161.42); 11 of 12 books ended below their $100 start, all 36 sensitivity cells negative, and the thread's advertised 80% win rate was not in the data.

sections.label: Forward Paper-Testing Tracks (September 2026)
items: Built three supervised forward paper-testing tracks — crypto, US stocks and Polymarket — all driven by Jev and paper-only end to end (no keys, no orders anywhere): a crypto track (two state variants over a 21-day window: a control replicating the earlier one-day test, plus a richer state carrying code-computed RSI-14, EMA-20/50, 15/60/240-minute changes, volume deltas and Jev's own last three answers per coin — first swept across ten decision cadences, then settled to a single 5-minute cadence once the replays had shown interval choice was noise); a stocks track (20 liquid US large caps, events from EDGAR filings — 8-K full text, 10-Q/10-K metadata — plus a daily per-ticker news digest, across filings-only, filings+news and price-state control books); and a Polymarket track (a daily scan of ~150 top open markets judged for resolution clarity, news staleness and P(yes), trading divergence across three books with the gates added one at a time).

Every track trades on the real market mechanics: Binance lot-size flooring with sub-$5 dust stranded and never sellable on crypto; whole-share flooring at a $500 clip with IBKR commission max($0.35, 0.35% of shares) per side on stocks; Polymarket's per-category taker-fee formula on $25 positions — max 10 open per book, resolutions within 30 days, held to settlement.

Anti-cheat timing by construction: a stock entry fills at the first open after max(event date, discovery date), so a simulated fill can never land at an open from before the answer that caused it, and the crypto comparator carries the same stranded-cash mechanics as the books it is measured against.

Production-shaped supervision: a continuous systemd service for crypto (restart-and-resume from its ledgers) plus persistent daily timers for stocks and Polymarket; per-track Jev spend caps enforced in code ($15 / $5 / $5); escalations queued to the trading agent profile over its Bot Chat (idle-checked, batched, at most one per 30 minutes); a daily digest posts each track's headline numbers, and a read-only dashboard shows the live books — wallet cards, equity charts and buy-and-hold comparators — with a 30-second auto-refresh. The tracks went live on 27 September 2026 and are still inside their first results window.

Extended the crypto track at the end of September with two confidence-gated books — act only when Jev's chosen action carries P≥0.70, else hold — running alongside the ungated controls so the gate earns forward evidence instead of another replay: logic-tested offline before a live restart, and both gated books are live with low-confidence actions already being skipped.

sections.label: Methodology
items: Explicit, documented limits — max drawdown, parameter-sweep selection bias, single-period caveat — results presented with the honest boundary of what the test does and does not prove

projects.title: RepLog — iOS Workout Tracker
projects.desc_html: A native iOS strength-training tracker written from scratch as a full alternative to a commercial lifting app, with an RPE column the original lacks — plus a small self-hosted sync service that mirrors finished sessions into one flat CSV an AI coaching agent can read.

sections.label: App
items: SwiftUI app on an iOS 26 target: Swift 6, a SwiftData on-device store, an XcodeGen project definition and zero third-party Swift packages — 39 source files, roughly 6,800 lines of Swift

All eight exercise types a real training log needs (weight × reps, weighted holds, added-load and assisted bodyweight, pure bodyweight reps and timed holds, cardio, note-only sets), plus supersets, drop sets, routines with warm-up and working schemes, a rest timer and repeat-workout from history

RPE column carried through every surface — active workout rows, saved sessions, exercise history, routine targets and the sync CSV; optional, half-point steps from 1.0 to 10.0, displayed as 8 rather than 8.0
Statistics hub on Swift Charts: per-exercise volume and estimated one-rep-max trends, personal records per rep range, seasonal bests and session records

Shipped 1.0.0 to the owner's iPhone and iterated on his feedback from daily use: a second round of six fixes made deleting a workout local-only (a session already in the sync database is never destroyed from the phone), kept an open workout finishable after leaving the editor, put a confirmation in front of "finish", gave the Log a manual sync control that reports its real state (up to date / relative time / auth failure), centred set cells under their exercise titles and dropped a dead settings section — each change carried by a new unit or UI test, with the simulator's offline drill reworked to assert the queued count is visible from the Log before a manual sync

Third round of owner feedback, from daily use in the gym (September 2026): routines lost the shared warm-up/working scheme, so a routine exercise is now a set count plus a note held per routine — the same lift reads "3×5, go light" in one routine and "4×4, no belt" in another — and that note is drawn on the routine row and carried into the workout from both start paths; a finished workout now opens the same editor as an active one, with no Finish control and no live timer (1.1.4 on the download page); and the set row was rebuilt against three candidate layouts put side by side in the simulator, shipping the winner after equalising the column gaps and centring the set-number circle on the row

Fourth round of owner feedback (October 2026): the keyboard bar gained ← → ✓ — chevrons step through every inline box in on-screen order, the check closes the keyboard, and the box being edited now scrolls clear of the software keys; shipped to the download page as 1.1.8, with the test gate green on the simulator (36/36 unit, 19/19 UI tests).
A store that fails to open starts a fresh file store instead of falling back to memory, so a damaged database can never masquerade as an empty training history

sections.label: Sync Service
items: lift-sync: a FastAPI service that upserts finished sessions into a single flat CSV — bearer auth, a single-writer lock, upsert by session ID, delete tombstones, atomic file rewrite, JSONL audit log and a health endpoint; 55 passing pytest tests, including two simultaneous uploads and an eight-thread upsert race
Ships as one Docker image with a compose file, and the CSV header is frozen so the file stays legible to a human and a model alike

Offline-first client: an outbox queues finished sessions and retries with backoff, tombstones deletions and guarantees a single upload per session — sync is optional and off by default, the phone stays the source of truth

sections.label: Distribution & Device Install
items: Over-the-air install path built from scratch: an ad-hoc Release archive exported on the Mac and published to a dedicated app-downloads LXC (Debian 12, 2 vCPU / 1 GB, container 111) running nginx over /srv/downloads with a cloudflared tunnel hostname, so a build reaches the phone by opening one URL in Safari — no cable, no Xcode and no Bonjour. Also established why the first attempt failed: signing needs the Mac's GUI session (launchctl asuser), because a plain SSH session cannot reach the signing keychain

One command publishes a build: publish.sh takes the IPA plus name, bundle id, version and base URL, writes the manifest.plist, a themed install page carrying the build's real identity (version, bundle id, size, build timestamp and the itms-services link) and a meta.json, then rebuilds the root index from every app's meta.json. Both pages are noindex, and ad-hoc signing limits installation to devices in the provisioning profile — a public URL that Apple's own distribution rules keep closed

sections.label: Migration & Testing
items: One-time importer over four years of the old app's export (6,524 set rows, 636 sessions, 88 exercises, 11 categories) that lifts RPE out of the free-text notes where it had been buried as bare numbers and ranges, and rewrites it as a real column

Whole Mac test gate green in a single run (Xcode 26.5, iPhone 17 Pro simulator): the build succeeds, 36 unit tests across 5 suites pass, and all 14 XCUITest cases pass — including an in-simulator offline drill that stops the sync service, finishes a workout, restarts the app, brings the service back, and proves exactly one upload, one tombstone and a 409 on re-import. The service's 55 pytest tests pass in the fast gate, and a scripted tour re-captures 30 screens in dark mode for screen-by-screen comparison against the 17 reference screenshots

The failing UI tests were real app defects, not flaky tests: session and exercise rows looked tappable but only the top row worked (a .plain button's hit target is the label's content shape, so taps landing under a Spacer did nothing) — pinned down by scanning tap coordinates across a row, then fixed with .contentShape(). Also found an iOS 26 toolbar clipping the Edit button to a single letter, a statistics screen that pushed and immediately popped back, and a test-reset flag that wiped the queued session mid-drill

Accessibility and Dynamic Type treated as evidence rather than assertion: the audit runs as its own test class at the largest accessibility text size, its 33 findings (contrast, hit areas under 44 pt, clipped labels) are logged as a known polish list instead of hidden, and everything a simulator cannot prove — HealthKit writes, Live Activities on a real lock screen, haptics — is listed as unverified rather than claimed

Testing policy changed on the owner's call (24 September 2026) and applied for the rest of the pass: end-to-end only — new behaviour is proven by UI tests that drive the app in the simulator and assert what is visible on screen, and the seven unit tests written for the routine-note rule were deleted the same day. The five older unit files stay only because they cover the sync engine and the maths a UI test cannot reach
Developed on a MacBook over SSH from the fleet host, driving the iOS simulator from the command line, with the implementation plan put through an adversarial review before any code was written

projects.title: Automated Video Production Pipeline
projects.desc_html: Code-first video pipeline that turns a researched script into a finished narrated history explainer — period imagery plus programmatic animation, rendered and assembled entirely in code.

sections.label: Pipeline
items: End-to-end build: researched script → per-scene narration → programmatic scenes → ffmpeg assembly. The reference episode — the Great Hunger (Ireland, 1845–51) — runs 3m22s at 1080p: 6,074 frames at 30 fps, H.264 video with stereo audio.

Visual mix keeps real context: period photographs, engravings and portraits sourced from Wikimedia Commons against a per-file licence manifest (39 public-domain files, the rest openly licensed or unrestricted), with maps plotted from Natural Earth data, charts and kinetic typography drawn programmatically where no imagery exists.

Narration tooled end-to-end: a purpose-built generator calls the ElevenLabs Brian voice (model auto-falls back v4 → v3 → multilingual v2), pulls the key at point of use from Bitwarden Secrets Manager, respells Irish-language names for the voice, and emits per-scene timing data that drives the renderer.
The renderer draws every frame with Pillow and streams them to ffmpeg; assembly produced the 1080p master plus a compressed preview cut, alongside three candidate thumbnail designs.

Extended the pipeline with browser-rendered motion: built RESONANCE, a self-contained one-shot 10-second canvas piece — a cymatics study with ~17,000 sand-grain particles settling into real Chladni standing-wave patterns, driven by a deterministic seek with a fixed seed. Proved the frame-exact capture path that can bring this class of animation into episodes: 120 deterministic frames captured over CDP at 1920×1080/30 fps, encoded with the pipeline's own libx264 settings into a 4.0-second MP4, verified by extracting frames back out of the encoded file.

sections.label: Agentic Pipeline
items: A second, fully agentic production line: a local model under an autonomous agent harness takes a single one-shot prompt from the researched dossier and brief to a finished, narrated film — script fact-checked against the dossier, ElevenLabs narration with per-scene timing, sourced imagery, a complete Remotion (React + TypeScript) project, the rendered MP4 and three thumbnail designs.

First episode complete: "Will Ireland Reunify? The Border Poll Explained" — 20 scenes, 12m51s, 23,116 frames at 1920×1080/30 fps, H.264 with the narration muxed in; charts drawn from eight data CSVs, SVG maps built from openly licensed county outlines, and 17 Wikimedia Commons images logged in a licence manifest.

Verified through the build: a fact-check bullet for every number, name and date in the script (57 in all), a readable proof frame for each of the 20 scenes, and a byte-identical re-render of one frame in two separate processes to pin determinism.

Being run as a controlled comparison across models and agent harnesses — the same episode produced once per run under an identical, hash-checked one-shot prompt, outputs kept side by side: local quants of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (base at 2-bit and 3-bit, the Swift 1.5 fine-tune at 2-bit) under the DeepSeek Harness and Hermes, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash under both harnesses. Ten finished episodes so far — each a complete film, 11m59s–13m51s.
